item.title: Controversial streamer Hasan Piker's lecture axed by University of Washington amid free-speech questions
item.description: Hasan Piker's canceled University of Washington lecture sparks a free speech debate as FIRE questions whether public backlash drove the decision.
item.content:encoded:
A University of Washington lecture featuring progressive Twitch commentator Hasan Piker is off, with school officials citing a flawed planning process as the reason for the cancellation.

Piker, a far-left streamer and YouTube personality, was set to appear in January as part of the school’s 2026-27 Speaker Series, the university said in a statement.

However, following "a review of the process by which the event was planned," the university canceled the event.

MARK HALPERIN CALLS HASAN PIKER A 'HORRIBLE PERSON' AS DEMOCRATS FACE PRESSURE TO DISTANCE FROM STREAMER

"It was determined that the process for organizing this event did not meet the necessary level of rigor for University-hosted events in the Speaker Series," the statement said.

"Going forward, procedures will be updated to ensure the standards we have for University-hosted events like the Speaker Series are met, particularly so that we can help elevate the level of dialogue on divisive topics during a polarized time in our country," it added.

The university’s cancellation of Piker, who previously said America "deserved 9/11" before later calling the remark "inappropriate," has prompted criticism from First Amendment advocates, with the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) condemning the move.

"If the decision was based on process — and not public backlash or criticism — @UW should be transparent about what standards were not met and how they were applied," the organization said in an X post.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

"Public universities can set standards for events. But they can’t use those standards as cover for canceling a speaker because of their views," it added.

Andrew Kolvet, the executive producer of the Charlie Kirk Show and a Turning Point USA spokesperson, said on X: "Let the radical Mao loving communist Hasan Piker speak, so long as he can resist the urge to call for the death of his political opponents. Universities do this to TPUSA often and blame some admin error etc. It’s wrong." 

Piker, a socialist, rose to fame following a series of controversial comments, and most recently faced backlash after he called for Democrats who are unsupportive of Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to face consequences for not holding the party line.

The popular streamer added that the party should use "Marxist-Leninist" punishment against anyone who fails to "follow the party line," but acknowledged that debate among the Democrats is expected in order to reach a decision.

HASAN PIKER CALLS FOR DEMOCRATS WHO OPPOSE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO BE 'PUNISHED'

His comments came just two days after El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination, narrowly defeating Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in the primary. Piker had previously appeared alongside El-Sayed on the campaign trail, who is set to face off against Republican nominee Mike Rogers in November.

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville, who has previously spoken out against Piker’s rhetoric, recently doubled down on his criticism of the podcaster.

"I am not going to be in the same party with Hasan Piker," Carville said on "The Sunday Briefing" earlier this month. "If he becomes a force in a Democratic Party, I'm out of here. I have no intention of ever being in the same political party with that guy."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Carville said that the Democrats will have to decide in the 2028 primary which direction it is headed in, as Piker’s viewpoints become more prevalent within the party.

FORMER DNC VICE CHAIR DAVID HOGG CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC MODERATES 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT VALUES'

"Everyone claims they're the ascendant ring, alright, on the 2028 presidential election, and this can only be resolved at the presidential level. It cannot be resolved at the state level," Carville told Fox News Digital. "And I am sure that there will be robust representation from the DSA ring of the party, whatever you want to call it. I'm sure there'll be a robust number of candidates from what I would call the governing wing of the Democratic Party, but you call it what you want."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Fox News Digital reached out to the University of Washington and Piker for comment.

Fox News Digital’s Alexander Hall and Rachel Wolf contributed to this report.

item.title: Nigeria's largest rescue operation frees 308 hostages held by militants in Kwara State
item.description: Victims of a six-month jihadi kidnapping in Nigeria's Kwara State describe starvation, forced births, and burying fellow captives in a forest hideout.
item.content:encoded:
Victims held for six months in captivity at the hands of jihadi kidnappers in Nigeria detailed on Friday the harrowing conditions they were kept in after being liberated in what Nigerian officials are calling the largest rescue operation in the country's history.

Nigerian forces rescued at least 308 victims from captivity in the past week, with the bulk of the victims coming from two distinct groups. 163 of the victims were taken from the Woro community in Nigeria's Kwara State in a Feb. 3 raid that saw their jihadi kidnappers kill an additional 160 people in the Woro village.

The victims told the Associated Press that they believed they had been taken as punishment for refusing to accept and acquiesce to the religious preachings of the jihadis.

One woman, Hauwa Saliu, told the outlet that her captors constantly asked the victims if they had accepted jihad yet.

NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

"We prayed to God to help us go back home, but it never really crossed our minds that we were going to go back home," she told the outlet.

Another victim, Amira Saliu, described the conditions in which the women and children were being kept, explaining that they were held in a forest near a river, and forced to put out fires and hide when they heard helicopters nearby.

FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY

Saliu, a nurse, also explained how she had to help 10 women give birth with no medical equipment or sanitary gloves.

"I had no choice but to use my bare hands," she told the outlet.

Mary Ishaya, 44, told the outlet that the captives often went days without food and had to bury other captives who had died.

"I still cannot find the right words to describe what has happened to us. We saw death and suffering," she said.

The governor of Kwara State, AbdulRahman AbdulRasaq, told reporters during a news conference that 46 victims were being treated at a hospital.

"This is indeed, indeed a very sad situation. We've not yet come to terms with it. We're still assessing the situation. As you can see, it's just kids ... children and women that are here today," he said. "It's truly a shame that this has happened."

COULD THIS AFRICAN NATION BECOME TRUMP'S NEXT TERROR TARGET AS JIHADISTS CLOSE IN ON POWER?

The incident highlights the ongoing tensions between Nigeria's militant Islamic insurgency in the north and the country's large Christian population, who make up roughly 45% of Nigeria's citizens.

On Christmas Day, President Donald Trump, in coordination with Nigeria's government, authorized precision missile strikes on Islamic State-affiliated groups in northern Nigeria, citing the need to protect the country's Christians.

The U.S. followed up in May, launching coordinated joint military action that reportedly resulted in the death of senior Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Mainuk.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: 'DEI queen': Virginia Dem's past embrace of far-left prosecutors unearthed
item.description: Shannon Taylor's record as Henrico County prosecutor clashes with her tough-on-crime campaign image as she seeks Virginia's 1st congressional district.
item.content:encoded:
Shannon Taylor, now the Democratic nominee in the race for Virginia’s First Congressional district, once endorsed progressive prosecutorial blueprints, advocating for less incarceration and more diversity as a Henrico County commonwealth attorney — some of the same "Democratic values" that ended in tragedy in other parts of Virginia.

Shortly after coming into the role in 2012, Taylor fired seven prosecutors under her.

"I stated publicly that the office needs to have more diversity and I’m going to keep to that public statement," Taylor said in an interview ahead of the firings.

Her track record is sparking criticism that she used her role to prioritize ideological and political views at the expense of public safety. It’s also clashing with portrayals from her campaign, highlighting her work as a tough-on-crime figure as she looks to win over a Republican-leaning district.

FORMER PROSECUTOR WHO ACCUSED TRUMP OF WEAPONIZING DOJ WINS DEM PRIMARY

Taylor highlighted her work as she topped a crowded field of Democratic candidates vying to challenge Republican incumbent Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Va.

"As Henrico’s top prosecutor for the last 14 years, Shannon has tried thousands of cases and put violent criminals, drug traffickers and abusers behind bars," Taylor states on her campaign website. "She has a record of shutting down fraudsters trying to take advantage of working families and locking up violent criminals who threaten our safety."

But that hasn’t always been the appearance she’s given.

After her seven firings, Taylor faced blowback for trying to hire a woman named Misty Whitehead as a police oversight prosecutor. However, before the role could be made official, social media posts from Whitehead surfaced that seemingly showed a pattern of attacking police.

Taylor faced backlash from the town’s county manager over her selected candidate.

"A county manager can’t tell a commonwealth’s attorney who to hire, but he can recommend whether or not local funds are included to supplement that salary. And in this case, I absolutely will not do it under any circumstances," County Manager John Vithoulkas said at the time.

Whitehead had a history of voicing concerns about police behavior and social justice that raised concerns for at least one county official, according to local reports.

Taylor defended her pick, telling local outlets that she believed the posts were "thoughtful analysis of the current events we are all living through."

Taylor also has ties to similarly-minded prosecutors in other counties — some of which entered the public eye recently due to tragic circumstances.

SPANBERGER'S ICE ROLLBACK TO BLAME FOR TODDLER KILLING, VIRGINIA 'HOTBED' OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME: DHS

In Fairfax County, Virginia, news broke that Abdul Jalloh, a 32-year-old illegal alien from Sierra Leone, stabbed a Virginia resident to death at a bus stop despite over 30 prior arrests and a known tendency for violent behavior.

Jalloh’s criminal record included charges of rape, malicious wounding, assault, drug possession, identity theft, trespassing, larceny and firing a weapon.

Even so, prosecutor Steve Descano had dropped many of them, prompting concern and outrage from lawmakers.

"You dismissed the case, and it’s shameful," Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C. said at a hearing where Descano was summoned to Congress to explain a series of similar cases.

Knott had been highlighting one such instance involving a child predator.

"When you dismiss a case, what happens to that defendant? He walks free. A disgusting, perverted individual preying on children, that you dismissed," Knott said.

Long before Descano’s time in the spotlight, Taylor had endorsed Descano, supporting his bid to become county prosecutor in 2019, citing shared outlooks.

"I am excited to endorse Steve Descano for Fairfax County’s Commonwealth’s Attorney because I know he will prioritize the same Democratic values we all share, making Fairfax a safe and just place for everyone and I am looking forward to working with him," Taylor wrote.

Taylor and Descano would go on to champion their shared values in a 2021 letter to the Biden Administration.

In it, the two joined 100 other district and county attorneys in championing a set of "21 principles for the 21st-Century prosecutor." The authors claimed that "tough on crime policies" had been "anathema to justice," championed an end to mandatory minimums and three-strike laws, advocated for taking immigration status into consideration when negotiating sentences and plea deals, and opposed calling rapists "rapists," drug dealers "drug dealers," and convicted criminals "felons" or "inmates."

"A number of elected reform-minded prosecutors are boldly redefining what it means to be a prosecutor," the letter states.

OKLAHOMA TEEN ACCUSED OF RAPING TWO GIRLS WALKS FREE; DA FURIOUSLY CALLS IN FEDS: ‘MADE MY BLOOD BOIL’

At least one Republican onlooker blasted Taylor’s record.

"She spent her time reshaping the prosecutor's office around identity politics, pushing a far-left agenda that put woke activism ahead of public safety, and fighting to turn Virginia into a far-left hellscape," Emma Hall, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Instead of prosecuting criminals and making Virginia safer, DEI queen Shannon Taylor chose to be a diversity, equity, and inclusion consultant."

Having secured the Democratic nomination, Taylor now heads to the general election on Nov. 3. Wittman, the district’s incumbent, last won re-election in 2024 in a 56.3% to 43.5% victory over Democratic challenger Leslie Mehta, an attorney.

item.title: Lawyer-turned-social media sensation is betting it all on God, love and grief
item.description: With a book deal and international tour ahead, Davide De Pierro explains how his car vlogs and Italian-American roots helped him earn 6 million followers — and growing.
item.content:encoded:
In a digital landscape often dominated by outrage, carefully curated perfection and fleeting trends, Davide De Pierro has built an audience by doing something refreshingly simple: telling honest stories about his experiences that make people feel seen. The New Jersey attorney-turned-digital creator joined Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview to discuss why authenticity — not algorithms — has become his greatest asset in a world where millions of people (six million who follow De Pierro, to be exact) are still searching for genuine human connection.

The 38-year-old was born in New Jersey and spent his early years in Italy before returning to Jersey City, where he still lives today. Though he continues to practice law at a family firm with his father and brother in Bloomfield, his career took a turn when he found success on TikTok and Instagram — pulling viewers in with his sometimes sarcastic, always profound reflections on work, life, love and faith.

"Being a person has been the same, always. What's changed is what you're wearing and what technology you're using," De Pierro said. "But really, I'm just talking about the human condition."

The self-described "half Italian/half Jersey boy" is now poised to re-release his self-published audiobook with HarperCollins in both a new audio edition and a hardcover version. The novel, "The Letters I Never Sent," will also heavily feature in his upcoming international tour, which will include stand-up comedy, live readings of excerpts from his book, a Q&A session and a meet-and-greet.

De Pierro is best known for his single-shot vlogs taken in his car, branded with captions like, "If I saw an alien I wouldn't even care honestly I got too much going on right now," "Started using my own money and realized my mom was right, we do have food at home," and "No matter what I have God."

On the heels of his life-changing success, De Pierro has remained humble — in fact, when asked what he believed made him so popular on social media, he found himself at a loss for words.

CANCEL ME IF YOU CAN: DAVE PORTNOY TAKES AIM AT CANCEL CULTURE CRITICS WHO 'ALREADY DECIDED' THE VERDICT

"I don't know why people are following me. I mean, I know what I do. I go on there and I talk about stuff. And maybe it's, in part, it could be the delivery. In part, it could be the actual language. In part, it could be the way my face looks in the car. I don't know. But I think it just happened."

"I'm happy that I won this little social media lottery, because otherwise I wouldn't be able to put my book out there and go on tour and meet people and have fun. And I'd be stuck in the law office all the time... Now I have to leave for other reasons, so my father permits me to go out and do a tour," he joked.

The creator described his success as "accidental" and said there was no "influencer strategy." Ironically, he used to consider himself "chronically offline."

"I was 37 years old. So, you know, I felt like that ship had sailed. I wasn't going to go dance on TikTok. Probably not for the best."

He credited an ex-girlfriend with the initial idea of posting his reflections on the internet.

"I thought that was a ridiculous idea. But I eventually took her advice, especially after the breakup — that's when men always take all the good advice from their exes. And it worked. And it kept working."

Millennials — the generation to which De Pierro proudly belongs — have been experiencing burnout for years, with research reported from Gallup to even the National Institutes of Health supporting the claim.

De Pierro told Fox News Digital he often posts about "workplace malaise," dating fatigue, and other kinds of exhaustion because he finds it's not just relatable, it's real.

"I think that you can't fake the authenticity of exhaustion. I think the relatability is that it's real. And so I am a person who has worked and who has gone through relationship problems. I'm not an inexperienced, younger man who's just kind of making things up that might be relatable. And I guess you just can't fabricate that kind of authenticity," said De Pierro, musing on how what some might call his late arrival to social media makes him stand out from other career influencers.

"The authenticity is not special, this isn't unique to me. I'm just describing what we all go through, but you have to go through it first. And so, certainly, there is an advantage to being a content creator in your late 30s if you're going to be talking about the struggles of being alive."

The TikToker pointed to the prolific nature and timelessness of William Shakespeare as an example of connection.

"What does he have in common with me, a 15th century English guy?" he posited in the wide-ranging interview. "In reality, he has everything in common with you, because he's a human being."

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

De Pierro's own audience is further evidence of this hypothesis, he said.

"My following is really a social experiment, if you look at it. I mean, there are people from all over the world and on all different spectrums. And I wonder if they know that they're following the same person, because I'm just talking about being a person. And everyone can relate to the experiences that we all go through every day, which are universal."

As a working attorney, De Pierro made it clear that his online ponderings should not be taken as legal advice.

"I would never call what I'm doing online advice. Especially being a lawyer, I'm so afraid of the word ‘advice.’ We never advise you unless you are our client."

"I don't want people to listen to it as advice. I'm not an expert on anything. I'm sharing observations, sharing experiences, sharing thoughts, but certainly not advice. No, don't do anything I say," he joked.

VIRAL BOY BAND INSISTS IT'S REAL AS IMMIGRATION FIGHT PUTS INTERNET FAME TO GOVERNMENT TEST

He attributed his contemplative style more to his Italian-American heritage than to his career in law, labeling Italians as "natural storytellers" and "expert complainers."

"I think it's part of the Italian identity to be a little bit playfully pessimistic. There might be even a superstition in that. You don't want to assume success."

"And so, I think that that plays into my character and my personality even in my videos. There's an exhaustion, there's a playful sense of pessimism there sometimes. A negativity almost. But it hides a more profound, I think, joy and optimism that Italians do have."

Despite referring to his portrayal in his social media videos as a "character," De Pierro told Fox News Digital that in the age-old Instagram vs. Reality — a concept that contrasts real-life with people's online personas — the lawyer-turned-comedian remains authentically himself.

"I mean, we all contain multitudes, right? So I think one of my personalities involves what I do in the car... All these little accents and modes of speaking are real to me. It depends on who I'm with. If I'm with my Jersey City friends, it's going to sound like "Goodfellas." But if I'm in a court of law, then I have to rein in it a little bit."

Add professional code-switcher to his growing list of accolades. 

Despite often baring his soul online, De Pierro said sharing his thoughts for all the world to see hasn't affected his personal life much — yet.

"It is real, it is authentic, and so it doesn't affect my life because I'm already being myself on camera. So it's not like I'm suddenly unrecognizable to my friends and family, they know that guy intimately," De Pierro maintained.

"But on the other hand — I'm not dating much — but I suspect that it will affect my dating, because I think people are starting to get the impression that I'm this enlightened man, and maybe they're going to have expectations of me in dating that are unrealistic.

"I'm just as much of an idiot as the men that I talk about in my videos."

JEFF FOXWORTHY PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON COMEDY'S CREATIVE PROCESS FOR WHAT COULD BE HIS LAST SPECIAL

It is always easier to give advice than to take it, he added.

"I'm still a person. And also, by the way, that wisdom is for everyone else. I'm just good at giving other people advice as opposed to living it myself. I've always been that friend that's really good at telling you what's wrong with you. But if I have to apply it to my own life, I'm probably going to fail nine times out of ten."

For someone who speaks openly about relationships and the roller coaster of emotions they bring, the Heartbreak Heartthrob reveals relatively little about the concrete details of his private life. 

That's intentional.

"What's funny about all this is that I'm incredibly public in the sense that I am constantly sharing my thoughts, but I'm almost never sharing my life. I'm just in the car. No one knows where I live. No one's ever seen my family. No one has ever seen the lower half of my body. So I'm extremely private while at the same time having a therapy session in my car," De Pierro told Fox News Digital.

De Pierro now speaks openly about many subjects with his growing following, but there is one he had to work his way up to: his faith.

He told Fox News Digital he is "100%" a Christian man, having gone to church every Sunday with his family all his life.

"My faith plays a huge role in my personal life. And so it was just a natural transition for me. As soon as I saw that I had this following and this kind of engagement, I thought, 'Wow, this is a perfect opportunity to speak about something that's really important to me.'"

De Pierro was inspired by the story of his grandfather, who died shortly after De Pierro was born.

FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA

"He was a preacher, and apparently — at least from the stories I've been told — a beloved man in the very small community that he lived and worked in. And a part of me thought, 'Here was this incredible man that I never met who only was able to speak to a few hundred people, maybe a thousand, over the course of his life.'"

"So I saw the opportunity that I had, and I thought to myself, 'Here I am, not even a tenth of the man that my grandfather was. And I have the opportunity to speak to millions of people at times. I have to use this opportunity, even if I could just plant a little seed of faith in these invisible people that are watching me from wherever they may be.'"

He has received no shortage of warm messages from viewers saying his posts have touched them and even helped them through hard times.

"And that's gratifying, too, of course, to feel like you're doing something more than just entertaining. Because it's great to get people to laugh and to get to feel seen and understood."

"But if you could also help people in a way that, again — it sounds crazy to me. I mean, I don't think that anything I'm doing is particularly helpful. But when I see those messages, I believe them. If they felt that way, then it's gratifying to know that I'm doing something, hopefully, useful."

HarperCollins imprint Hanover Square Press announced Monday it is set to publish De Pierro's debut novel, "The Letters I Never Sent," now on pre-sale and set for print and ebook publication on December 8, 2026. The audiobook version, De Pierro told FOX, will be available this October. Additionally, he will embark on his first-ever stand-up tour beginning late September.

The writer, performer, and viral content creator also shared his biggest icks and ticks, what he really thinks of modern dating, and the best advice he's ever received with Fox News Digital. But when asked if he had one final message he'd want to leave behind for his followers, it's a sentiment as refreshingly simple as he is: "God loves you."

item.title: Carmen Electra says 'Baywatch' pushed boundaries without crossing the line: 'It wasn't porn'
item.description: Carmen Electra reveals what made the original "Baywatch" a global phenomenon while promoting the new competition show, "Nation's Dumbest" on Fox.
item.content:encoded:
Carmen Electra is reminiscing about her days starring in the original "Baywatch."

In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old "Nation's Dumbest" contestant discussed the success of the original series, saying, all "the cast members made it special."

"It's hard to replace Pamela [Anderson] and Yasmine [Bleeth] and all those people. And there was just a certain tone. I don't know how to explain it," she said. "It had a certain tone to it that it was just such a fantasy, and maybe it was the first time on television you could see so much skin because we really were playing lifeguards right so we could be in these skimpy outfits."

She went on to say that the show possibly left people thinking, "Oh my God, what is this? We can see nipples."

BROOKS NADER SIZZLES IN ICONIC RED SWIMSUIT AS SHE SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES SNAPS FROM 'BAYWATCH' REBOOT SET

"And it wasn't porn. You know, what I mean? They didn't have to sneak away and find a VHS tape to like, sneak and put in. You can watch this," she added. "You can also learn something. Because, we heard from a lot of people, a lot of fans out there, that they learned so much watching the show."

Electra credited the show's sexy nature as one of the reasons it became the global phenomenon it is, saying they were "sometimes trying to be sexy, sometimes not trying to be sexy" and that "all of a sudden, you get these guys on there with these gorgeous bodies."

In addition to the sexy aspect of the show, Electra attributed its success to the fact that fans could learn something from the show, including how to give CPR, adding she also "learned how to give CPR," and joked, "I could save someone right now if I needed to."

The actress and model joined the show in 1997 for its eighth season, after gaining exposure from posing for Playboy in a 1996 pictorial.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

In terms of returning for the new reboot of the series, Electra is open to putting on the iconic red one-piece once again, since her former love interest on the show, David Chokachi has signed on to return.

"I could do something. Come in, have another love scene with David Chokachi. Just something really cute and fun. I would be down to get into the water again," she said. "I think it would be fun it makes sense I was David Chokachi's love interest way back then. I think it would be really fun and why not, you know?"

His character, Cody Madison, is now the owner of a beachside bar, The Shoreline, and also acts as a mentor to the younger new lifeguards.

"I think it would be so cool if I just came in for an episode to surprise him and say hi. They fall in love again, who knows," Electra said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

One thing the actress is not willing to go through again is "the schooling that I did when I first joined the cast," noting, "that was really tough."

Following her time on "Baywatch," Electra had a successful career in both film and television, appearing in films such as "Scary Movie," "Cheaper by the Dozen 2," "Meet the Spartans" and others.

She also recently appeared as a contestant on "Nation's Dumbest," a new celebrity competition show. She told Fox News Digital she originally didn't want to do it, saying, "I didn't pay attention in school" and that she "didn't have a good feeling about it."

"Fox kept getting on the phone. They're like, it's gonna be so easy. It's gonna be fun. It's like acting think of it as an acting role," she said. "Once I was not there anymore, I kind of missed it...and there was a lot of fun. I did miss the cast a lot but yeah, I think we were all sitting there going, 'What? Why the hell did we subject ourselves to be on this show?'"

"I definitely had a lot of anxiety and I would freeze. As soon as we would have to rush and say something, answer a question really fast or there was something weird we had to do," she added. "It could be very stressful and I would freeze."

When it came to a moment that still haunts her, Electra couldn't believe she couldn't remember what BBL stood for, saying the producers threw in "a really easy question that she's gonna get and I got it wrong. I couldn't believe it."

The show features celebrity contestants who undergo pop quizzes and physical challenges with the ultimate goal of being eliminated as early as possible, in order to avoid being the last one standing and being named the nation's dumbest.

Electra was ultimately eliminated after the fourth episode of the show, which aired on Aug. 5.

item.title: $20 avocado toast fuels outrage as travelers say airport food prices are out of control
item.description: An avocado toast item for nearly $20 at an airport in the South sparked outrage, but an industry expert says high rents and limited options are responsible for driving up airport food prices.
item.content:encoded:
Travelers are increasingly questioning why a quick bite at the airport can come with a restaurant-level price tag, according to several reports.

A recent viral post on X added to the frustration after a traveler slammed a nearly $20 avocado toast purchased at an airport in the South.

The traveler said the $19.64 breakfast was supposed to include toasted sprout bread, avocado, extra virgin olive oil, bacon and crushed red pepper — but many commenters said the dish looked far less appetizing than the price suggested.

CROWDED AIRPORT LOUNGES FORCE AIRLINES TO RETHINK FUTURE OF TRAVEL PERKS FOR FLIERS

California chef and restaurateur Andrew Gruel looked at photos of the avocado toast and said he was not impressed.

"It [is] probably sold as avocado purée. ... They took a disposable plastic knife, and they wiped it on a piece of toast," Gruel told Fox News Digital in an interview.

"But it doesn't surprise me, and I don't put it on the actual worker who made that," he added as he shared his personal point of view.

AIRPORT LOUNGE CHAOS GOES VIRAL AS KIDS RUN WILD AND PASSENGERS DITCH BASIC ETIQUETTE

Gruel believes the quality of food at airports is going down as the prices are going up.

"Nowadays, all you're getting is just prepackaged, co-packed foods at airports," he said.

"You'll have one vendor that's going to prepackage sandwiches and wraps and hard-boiled eggs, and maybe some meat and cheese platters," he added.

Gruel said he believes much of the food at sit-down restaurants in airports is "overpriced garbage."

THE BIGGEST FOOD AND DRINK MISTAKES TRAVELERS MAKE ON FLIGHTS, EXPERTS WARN

"That is rarely cooked from scratch," he said. But "I don't want to say that there's no good food at airports."

Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From the Wing" told Fox News Digital that the issue goes beyond one expensive breakfast that's been called out on social media.

Airport restaurants contend with higher rents, limited storage space, stricter security requirements for deliveries and higher labor costs, all of which contribute to higher menu prices, Leff and Gruel said.

"It's expensive to operate there," Leff said.

CO-PILOT BECOMES SICK MIDAIR AS CREW ILLNESS REPORTS EMERGE AFTER OVERNIGHT LAYOVER

He added that some airports advertise "street pricing," but the wording isn't always clear.

"They never really tell you which street," Leff said.

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey even allows airport concessionaires to charge up to 15% more than comparable off-airport "street prices," according to the official Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Concessionaire Street Pricing Standards and Procedures Manual.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"More expensive, not as good," Leff said about all airport food in general.

The pricey avocado toast is far from the only expensive item travelers find at airport restaurants.

A burger at Paris Cafe in New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport costs $34, according to the restaurant's online menu.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Barney's Beanery at Los Angeles International Airport charges $21.30 for its Barney Breakfast, which includes eggs, hash browns and toast, according to the airport's Shop & Dine website.

"Even if you just want a bottle of water, you're paying $5 or $6 for a cheap bottle," Gruel said. "That's where they're making their money."

The viral avocado post prompted travelers to share their own frustrations.

"Airport food prices are absolutely out of control," one Reddit user wrote.

"Breakfast burrito to go ... $36 bucks. I thought maybe I broke a window or something, and they added that on," one Reddit user quipped.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

While some airport lounges offer quality meals, Leff said he wouldn't recommend purchasing lounge access just for the food. 

Gruel agreed. "I'd say be careful of the airport lounge food because, most of the time, it's just sitting out there, you know, under a sneeze guard and everybody's putting their hands all over it," he said.

Leff suggested eating before arriving at the airport or bringing food from home.

Additional advice: Look for sandwiches.

"I would never spend $25 on pizza like that. But I've actually had a few good sandwiches at airports," Gruel said.

He added, "Tortas Frontera, which is Rick Bayless's shop in Chicago's [O'Hare] airport — they make a pretty good sandwich. Granted, it's $25 for a sandwich, maybe $20, but it's a good quality product."

item.title: The WNBA has limited options after two men declared for the draft, and those options aren't great
item.description: Enes Canter Freedom and Royce White declared for the 2027 WNBA Draft, claiming transgender identity and forcing the league into a no-win situation.
item.content:encoded:
Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White put the WNBA in an almost impossible spot on Friday when they declared for the 2027 Draft in the wake of the Sophie Cunningham drama, and the ways out are limited.

Frankly, none of them are great for the league, which is, presumably, the point. Unless, of course, both former NBA stars are just itching to get back in the game of basketball.

I doubt it, though.

FORMER NBA PLAYER ROYCE WHITE SAYS HE IS DECLARING FOR NEXT WNBA DRAFT AFTER ENES KANTER ANNOUNCEMENT

For those who missed it, Kanter and White called the WNBA's bluff by both declaring their intention to enter next year's draft within hours of each other Friday evening.

"If simply declaring who you are is all that’s required, then I meet every requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," Freedom stated in a social media post.

"I'm transgender. I'm a woman. I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball, professional basketball, so I'll be declaring for the WNBA draft in 2027 as well," White later added. "They’re going to have nightmares, and they should. I really feel like I’m going to be dominant."

What a moment for those two! Trailblazers. They'll be like modern-day Jackie Robinsons next year when they hear their names called.

Of course, there is a long way to go to get to that point. A loooooooooong way. It's more likely than not that it never happens, which I'm assuming both guys (girls?) would prefer.

That would mean the WNBA stepped in and told both they were not eligible for the draft because they are very clearly not women. That's the best case scenario for them, and the worst case for the WNBA.

It would shatter all the performative nonsense they've shoved down our throats for the past month/year/decade.

So, here are a couple options forward, best I can tell ...

This is probably the cleanest break, and it's certainly in the WNBA's wheelhouse. The league is rudderless. They could simply come out and say, "We're aware of two former NBA players recently declaring for next year's draft. They are ineligible under the current league rules. We have no further comment."

Refusing to elaborate is the best play for the league, mainly because the "reporters" who cover the WNBA are shills for the league and refuse to ask any actual questions. I can assure you that most of them are disgusted by White and Freedom, and would love this story to go away. They will most likely play ball.

OutKick is already basically banned from most WNBA events at this point, so don't depend on us asking them to elaborate. They wouldn't let us get within a MILE of a WNBA facility after making this statement.

Dan Zaksheske's face would be plastered on the walls of every locker room. Jon Root would have a restraining order out on him around every WNBA arena. It would be the most non-inclusive inclusive league of all time.

I can't believe I just wrote the word "cisgender." Lordy. What a time to be alive.

Cisgender means a person's gender identity matches the sex they were identified as at birth. The league could say the two have publicly lived and identified as men, rather then as transgender women, and therefore don't meet the draft requirements.

WNBA STAR SAYS SHE WOULD WELCOME A TRANS PLAYER TO HER TEAM, AND THEN SAYS SOMETHING EVEN DUMBER

Those requirements are laid out in Article XIII, Section 1(a) of the WNBA Collective Bargaining Agreement. They say, "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but doesn't define the word "woman" and there is nothing about gender identification.

Not a very inclusive bargaining agreement for a league that prides itself on it. Tisk tisk.

The WNBA probably won't go this route because the immediate follow-up question would be, "Fine. What distinguishes an eligible transgender woman from Enes Kanter Freedom?"

Again, you'd need actual media in the room to ask that question, so perhaps the league can explore this option.

Another fun one! The league could scramble and put a clause into the rulebook that outlines who can and cannot play in the WNBA.

For example, something along the lines of, "Trans women can only enter the draft after showing proper transition history and hormone levels." The league could create some sort of criteria out of thin air — most of these trans arguments are created out of thin air, so this would be easy — and wiggle their way out of the mess that way.

If they go this route, they get to remain the proper level of woke, but also keep White and Freedom out of the league ... for now.

This kicks the can down the road.

I call this the "I-4 of routes." For those who live in Florida, you know that Interstate 4, which runs through the middle of the state, is a hellscape. I believe at one point, it was the deadliest highway in America.

It's horrible. I've seen things happen on that interstate that still give me the shivers to this day.

The trans community would be furious. The left would revolt. It would be anarchy.

Remember, this is the league that has made trans rights its "battle," as Golden State star Gabby Williams stated earlier this summer. Saying Freedom and White can't play because they are biological men would shatter the entire narrative. It would be over.

This is the easiest and sanest route to take, which means the WNBA will do what most Florida folks do and avoid I-4 at all costs.

Finally, the league could just lean into this and let the chips fall where they may. This is the nuclear option. This is the WNBA simply refusing to bow down to sanity and instead lean into the skid.

The whole "trans rights" movement has been the left's proverbial hill to die on for years now. YEARS. There is simply no going back now. They can't. If they pivoted, it would undo everything.

Also found in Davis' home were handwritten notes depicting the construction of weapons and an apparent drawing of what appeared to be a Molotov cocktail, according to photos released by the sheriff's office.

Other items of concern found by authorities in Davis' home included a U.S. Army improvised munitions handbook and a copy of "The Anarchist Cookbook," a 1971 book that contains instructions on how to make explosives, weapons and illicit drugs.

Hardwick said Davis and his friend had planned to rob someone named CJ, though investigators have been unable to determine who CJ is.

Based on this evidence, plus online searches by Davis, Hardwick said there was a "much bigger picture than just a robbery of that individual."

NEW VIDEO SHOWS OKLAHOMA HIGH SCHOOL PRINCIPAL TACKLING GUNMAN WHO OPENED FIRE INSIDE THE SCHOOL

"Davis was using his devices in his home to research things. He had a [fixation] with people that had committed these mass school shootings, people that have gone in and done these mass stabbings," Hardwick said. Davis is still in custody at the St. Johns County Jail on a $240,000 bond, the sheriff said. He pleaded not guilty to the charges against him and is scheduled to be arraigned again next month.

Davis' friend, with whom he was texting about the alleged robbery, spent 21 days in the Florida Department of Juvenile Justice before being released, the sheriff said.

Neither of the boys will be allowed to return to their school. St. Johns County School District deputy superintendent Paul Abbatinozzi clarified there was never a direct threat to Switzerland Point Middle School.

item.title: 'Seinfeld' star Patrick Warburton says making out with Carol Burnett felt 'like kissing mom'
item.description: Patrick Warburton recalls making out with Carol Burnett at 27, plus his unexpected encounters with Betty White and Bea Arthur over the years.
item.content:encoded:
Before Patrick Warburton became a fan favorite as David Puddy on "Seinfeld," he found himself in an unlikely role: Carol Burnett's much younger lover.

On "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," the actor recalled what it was like being paired with the legendary comedienne in a skit.

"I made out with her," he told Sibilia. "I was 27 at the time, and she played a soap star. She played the good sister, the good twin and the evil twin. They were both dating the same toy boy, which was 27-year-old me."

At the time, Burnett was in her late 50s.

CAROL BURNETT REVEALS WHAT SHE MISSES ABOUT COMEDY: ‘I DON’T THINK A NETWORK WOULD TAKE A CHANCE’

"I’d have scenes where I was making out with the good one and the bad one, [and they] were both Carol," he explained.

"Carol was adorable. When we’re doing that, she looks to the director and goes, ‘Oh, we’re going to have to rehearse this some more.’ That was very cute and very sweet."

"For me, it was kind of like kissing mom because I grew up with the family on ‘The Carol Burnett Show,’" he continued. "But it is funny as I look back. I made out with Carol Burnett. ... Me and the older gals, I don’t know!"

WATCH: PATRICK WARBURTON RECALLS KISSING CAROL BURNETT AT AGE 27

The 61-year-old joked there appeared to be a trend.

"I had a 94-year-old Betty White rub my naked chest down in bed in a show," Warburton told the outlet. "I have very interesting Eartha Kitt stories. Nothing too lascivious, but it’s just odd."

Another "Golden Girls" legend kept Warburton on his toes.

"I remember Bea Arthur was doing a three-episode arc on a TV show I was doing, and I was about 27 at the time when I did that as well," he explained. "There were about seven or eight of us that were all supposed to go get sushi for lunch. Everybody backed out. Bea Arthur looks at me, and she goes, ‘I want sushi, don’t you?’ And I go, ‘Well, yeah, I wanted it.’ And she goes, ‘You and I will go.’"

"So now I'm having lunch with Bea Arthur, and I'm 27," he continued. "Bea was lovely, but as we all know, Bea was also — there was just something kind of scary and imposing about that woman. And the character she played was not one to be trifled with.

"And I just felt very uncomfortable just sitting there at first having lunch with Bea. [But] we had a lovely lunch. She mostly talked about rescuing greyhound dogs because that was her cause. It's just weird, Joe. Me and the older gals, I don't know!"

Warburton later became a fan favorite as Puddy on the '90s sitcom "Seinfeld" and has voiced paraplegic police officer Joe Swanson on Seth MacFarlane's "Family Guy" since 1999.

Warburton previously spoke to Fox News Digital about how his parents, John and Barbara Warburton, had a particularly strong dislike of "Family Guy."

"They don't see it as satire. They see it as blasphemy," Warburton said. "So, it was just a conversation that we were never really able to have. We never saw eye to eye on it. But, yeah, they always hated that show."

WATCH: PATRICK WARBURTON DISCUSSES RELIGIOUS BACKGROUND AND FINDING OUT SECRET HERITAGE

Warburton said his parents objected to the animated series on moral grounds because they were "very religious." John, who died in 2018, spent three months at the Abbey of Our Lady of Gethsemani in Bardstown, Kentucky, where Thomas Merton was his spiritual advisor. He nearly became a monk before deciding to pursue a career in medicine.

According to Warburton, Barbara shared her husband's devout Catholic faith and his strong disapproval of their son's most popular shows.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"If Mom could possibly be worse than Dad, she is, yes," Warburton joked.

Warburton recalled that his mother's religious convictions led to another attempt to influence his work.

"I remember back in the day when we lived in Woodland Hills, my mom and dad came to visit. And we were in the kitchen, and my mom says, 'Are you going to work on "Seinfeld" today?' And I said, 'I am, as a matter of fact.' And she said, ‘I have this dynamic videotape that has converted a lot of my Jewish friends. If I gave it to you, would you give it to Jerry?’" Warburton recalled with a laugh.

Warburton said his mother didn't easily give up on her goal of converting Jerry Seinfeld to Catholicism.

"Years later, Jerry was performing [stand-up] in Pensacola, Florida," Warburton said. "And mom and dad wanted to go. And I go, 'I'll hook you up.' So, I call up Jerry, get them a couple of tickets. So, I talked to my mom after the show, and I go, ‘Did you enjoy Jerry?' And she goes, ’He was wonderful. I even wrote him a lovely thank-you letter.'

"And, at that point, that's when the hair on the back of my neck stood up, and I go, 'You probably didn't just leave a letter, did you, Mom? You probably left a DVD.' And she goes, ‘I did,'" Warburton continued. "I go, ‘Do you know how disrespectful that is?’ And she said, ‘I only answer to one person, the Lord above.’ So, that's how they operate. That's how Mom operates."

Warburton told Fox News Digital he later brought up his mother's unexpected gift when he ran into Seinfeld in New York.

"We had a laugh, but yeah, I'm sure he didn't watch it," he said.

"He hasn't converted yet, as far as I know."

Though Warburton has previously described himself as a "bad Catholic," he told Fox News Digital he has "absolutely" had moments when he felt uncomfortable with some of his work because of his faith.

"Catholic guilt runs deep," he acknowledged. "But I believe God has a sense of humor."

Fox News Digital's Ashley Hume contributed to this report.

item.title: 'One Night Only' Review: Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner charm in lively high-concept rom-com
item.description: Fox News Digital reviews Universal Pictures' high-concept romantic comedy "One Night Only" starring Callum Turner and Monica Barbaro. Directed by Will Gluck.
item.content:encoded:
Let's talk about sex — yes, seriously. It's kind of important for this review. 

We live in a time when fewer people are getting married and more people — particularly Gen Zers — aren't having sex, which is why it's interesting that a movie like "One Night Only" is being released now.

In an alternative America, Congress passed a law banning premarital sex except for one night only (get it?) every year. Think "The Purge," but with casual sex instead of committing heinous crimes. The crackdown is quite serious; everyone has a sensor on their wrists so that the police can track and arrest anyone who attempts hanky-panky while unwed during the rest of the year.

All the singletons in New York City treat the sex ban carve-out like a holiday; people take off work early, there are parties everywhere, there's even a New Year's-esque countdown to kick it off. You'll find couples making out at every street corner or bar, or spot them getting it on through the window. The aspiring lovers have just 12 hours to get it on and, if they're lucky, find their soulmate.

‘SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY’ REVIEW: TOM HOLLAND, ZENDAYA RETURN FOR ACTION-PACKED, EMOTIONAL SEQUEL

Pizzeria owner Owen (Callum Turner) was hoping to have a romantic evening with his longterm girlfriend (Maya Hawke of "Stranger Things" fame) — until she dropped a bomb that she wants to try sleeping with one of their neighbors. His "one night only" was ruined before it could even begin.

Meanwhile, an aspiring singer, Allie (Monica Barbaro), was supposed to go out with a friend until she ditched her for a guy seemingly within minutes of going to a bar. Now she's forced to navigate the night on her own.

Obviously, we know what happens next. They have a chance encounter, they go their separate ways, their adventurous evenings repeatedly bring them back together, hijinks and hilarity ensue, yada yada yada. 

'THE ODYSSEY' REVIEW: CHRISTOPHER NOLAN GOES EPIC WITH HIS MOST AMBITIOUS FILM TO DATE

The premise is kind of absurd on its face. On paper, this is a dystopian nightmare and a widespread rebellion to fight the mandate would erupt (folks make it clear they're unhappy with the now three-year-old law). But it remarkably works as a romantic comedy thanks in part to the universe created by screenwriter Travis Braun, who notably makes his feature debut following an IDMB credit list ironically filled with children's programming ("Pupstruction," "Vampirina," "Muppet Babies" etc.). 

Past films by director Will Gluck ("Easy A," "Friends with Benefits," "Anyone But You") haven't exactly landed with me despite the fanfare they've gotten over the years, but "One Night Only" rises above the rest because he's able to lean into the silliness of the universe Owen and Allie live in, which includes a desperate search for a condom since they're sold out virtually everywhere.  

AS ‘THE ODYSSEY’ THRIVES AT THE BOX OFFICE, FRANCHISE FATIGURE HITS SUMMER WITH BOMBS LIKE ‘SUPERGIRL,’ ‘MOANA’ 

Turner, known for his roles in "Masters of the Air," the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise and more recently another high-concept rom-com (2025's "Eternity"), fits the bill as an on-screen heartthrob, toeing the line between cocky and endearing. Barbaro, who you might remember from "Top Gun: Maverick" and "A Complete Unknown" — the latter earning her an Oscar nomination, shines as the gorgeous yet down-to-earth Allie. 

Barbaro showcasing her vocal talents after appearing as Joan Baez in the Bob Dylan biopic is an added bonus (a note to Hollywood: cast her in a musical already).

"One Night Only" isn't exactly "When Harry Met Sally" or "Sleepless in Seattle," but it's thoroughly entertaining and has plenty of decent laughs. Aside from the wild cameo appearances of Gluck's famous pals, two of the best scene stealers are Molly Ringwald and LeVar Burton, who play Owen's mom and her "one night only" lover.   

'THE INVITE' REVIEW: SETH ROGEN, OLIVIA WILDE HOST ONE HILARIOUS DINNER PARTY YOU WON'T REGRET ATTENDING

Comedies over 90 minutes tend to overstay their welcome, so "One Night Only" might've benefited by shaving some of its runtime. Precious minutes didn't need to be allotted to the overt product placement, namely Durex and K&Y. 

"One Night Only" is a satirical examination of casual sex in the form of an amusing, raunchy rom-com, marking Gluck's best film to date and elevating up-and-comers Turner and Barbaro as capable lead performers. It's a solid date night option perhaps for younger couples — otherwise, it's probably best to save this for a night in.  

"One Night Only" is rated R for sexual material, language and brief nudity. Running time: 1 hour, 42 minutes. In theaters now.

item.title: Common marriage habit could quietly kill your sex life, expert warns
item.description: A clinical sexologist reveals the everyday habits that quietly kill intimacy and explains how couples can work together to reignite desire.
item.content:encoded:
Sexual desire can change over the course of a marriage, particularly with age and major life changes — and research suggests certain lifestyle and relationship factors may also contribute to a lower libido.

But changes in desire or frequency do not necessarily mean a couple’s sex life is unhealthy, according to experts.

Dr. Anna Elton, a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said there is "no medically prescribed number that defines a healthy sex life."

HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA

"What's healthy is whether both partners feel connected, satisfied and respected in their intimate relationship," she told Fox News Digital.

"For some couples, that may mean several times a week, while for others it may be once or twice a month. The healthiest benchmark is mutual fulfillment."

Rather than comparing their sex lives to those of others, Elton encouraged couples to define what is healthy for their own relationship.

"Talk about what feels satisfying, how much time can pass before one or both of you starts feeling disconnected and what your warning signs are," she said. "Once you've agreed on that range, make a commitment to maintain it together."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Elton advised couples not to let too much time pass without "intentionally reconnecting," as prolonged disconnection can take a toll on the relationship.

"If we simply wait until the mood is perfect or the stars align, work, children and everyday responsibilities usually get in the way," she said. "Healthy relationships require intention. Both partners should share responsibility for initiating connection and creating the conditions where desire can develop."

For many couples, building careers, raising children, caring for aging parents, managing finances and juggling other responsibilities can demand more of their attention — and they may not realize that the relationship itself has become a low priority.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"As a result, couples begin living parallel lives," Elton told Fox News Digital. "Conversations revolve around schedules, errands, bills and the kids. Intentional time together becomes less frequent. Affection, physical touch, flirting and playfulness become less frequent, replaced by stress, conflict and growing resentment."

"For many couples, those changes are among the earliest signs that the relationship is no longer being intentionally nurtured, and sexual intimacy declines soon afterward."

Elton countered that many couples she's worked with continued to have sex regularly to "keep the peace or avoid conflict." While their sex life appeared healthy from the outside, the couples felt "emotionally disconnected and unfulfilled."

"Physical intimacy and emotional closeness go hand in hand," she said. "If we want to improve our sex lives, we have to focus on the connection itself."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If one or both partners consistently feel rejected, lonely or resentful, or avoid conversations about intimacy altogether, it's time to seek help."

If sex becomes painful or erectile difficulties arise – or if hormonal concerns, trauma, depression, anxiety or persistent differences in desire are creating distress – couples should address these issues with a professional as early as possible, the expert advised.

One of the most common concerns Elton sees in her practice is differences in sexual desire, which she confirmed is "completely normal."

The key is to approach intimacy "as a team," as research has shown this leads to maintaining "stronger desire" over time.

"Being responsive means staying curious about your partner's experience," she said. "Instead of pressuring or withdrawing, couples communicate openly, respect each other's boundaries and work together to find an approach to intimacy that feels satisfying for both people."

Couples should also broaden their definition of intimacy, Elton suggested, as general affection, physical touch, flirting, emotional closeness and intentional time together can "help partners feel more connected and create the conditions where sexual desire naturally returns."

item.title: Georgia ICE sweep nabs over 700 criminal illegal aliens including sex offenders, child abusers
item.description: Operation Safe Community in Atlanta, Georgia netted over 1,200 immigration arrests, with DHS saying 720 had criminal histories including sex crimes.
item.content:encoded:
Federal immigration officers arrested more than 1,200 illegal immigrants in the Atlanta, Georgia area, including 720 who DHS said had been convicted of or charged with crimes.

Speaking on "Fox & Friends," Marcos Charles, executive associate director of ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, said the sweep took violent criminals — including sex offenders and child abusers — off the streets.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

"We're talking about sex crimes, assault and battery, some with DUI convictions, domestic violence. These individuals needed to be taken off the street, not only because they're criminals, but because they are here illegally in the United States," he added.

The Department of Homeland Security announced online that the sweep, called "Operation Safe Community – Atlanta," focused on criminal illegal immigrants. 

"Every day, the men and women of ICE ERO were out in the streets across the nation, enforcing the immigration laws as set forth by Congress. So we're keeping the community safe. We're [going to] be traveling all over the United States doing the same thing," Charles said.

TRUMP DHS CHIEF UNDER FIRE FROM CONSERVATIVES AFTER IMMIGRATION SPEECH IGNITES BACKLASH

"What we've done is we've adapted to that, not only with additional training, but we've adapted our methodology on how we conduct these enforcement efforts and our arrest methods," he said.

Among those arrested, DHS identified a Mexican national with prior convictions for "conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine and driving while intoxicated."

item.title: Protect College Sports Act stalls in overnight Senate showdown, vote pushed to September after chaotic evening
item.description: The Protect College Sports Act stalled Friday as senators filed amendments targeting conference realignment, women's sports, and NCAA liability.
item.content:encoded:
What looked like a last-minute lifeline for the 'Protect College Sports Act' turned into a 2 a.m. Senate dead end, even in spite of a late push from President Donald Trump.

After a frantic Friday filled with amendments, objections and pressure from the President to keep lawmakers in Washington, supporters believed they had a path to a vote before the August recess.

Senators and aides were called back to the Capitol late Friday night as momentum appeared to be building.

But in the early morning hours on Saturday, that push came up short. Unfortunately for Senators Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., along with Eric Schmitt, R-Mo, they could not garner enough support for a vote.

TED CRUZ URGES SENATE TO STAY IN WASHINGTON UNTIL PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT PASSES THIS WEEK

"The Protect College Sports Act continues to show great momentum. Sens Cruz and Schmitt have worked tirelessly with the support of nearly every conference in the country, HBCUs and the Olympic sports committee. It's clear that this bill is the only way to save college sports and women’s sports," Cruz and Schmitt said in a statement early Saturday morning.

"While we are disappointed that we could not get the unanimous consent agreement to finish this week, we locked in a guaranteed vote in September. With the strong support of President Trump, we look forward to him signing the bill on college game day in the Fall."

In what turned out to be an intense day of negotiations, Senators from both sides of the aisle met numerous times to discuss the legislation that kept college athletic officials and reporters glued to their phones over the previous 72 hours.

When the SEC and Big Ten voted to put their support behind the bipartisan legislation just one week ago, there was hope among everyone involved that they could get the bill to the Senate floor and send it to the House before the congressional recess.

On Friday, with the deadline creeping up on those looking to push this legislation through, a bevy of amendments were filed by Senators looking to enhance the bill in their eyes.

After days of anticipation about whether this 'NIL Bill' would actually be taken up for a vote, Senate aides were scrambling early Saturday morning to make their way back to the Capitol.

But, the intense negotiations turned into all sides laying down their swords, until September.

"Time may have run out to protect college sports in August, but there is plenty of time in September," Senator Maria Cantwell said in a statement. "I'm glad Senator Thune set a date certain in September to bring it up because the challenges facing student athletes and universities aren't going away.

"The Protect College Sports Act provides stability and gives first-ever federal NIL rights and scholarship and healthcare protections for athletes. And this bipartisan bill is how we protect women's and Olympic sports. I look forward to its passage in September."

Even with a push from President Donald Trump, this legislation was fighting against time, objections and the Senate 'hotline' that is used to essentially determine whether a bill would actually have the support to be voted on.

It was actually Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) who filed the most intriguing amendment to the PCSA, taking issue with the five-year independent section that would force schools to abandon their conferences, like the ACC, for a number of years before being allowed to join another.

This has been an issue discussed by many across the ACC and Big 12 in previous weeks, wondering aloud what this would prevent in terms of being raided by the others, most notably the SEC.

Right now, under its current form, conferences would only be allowed to have 19 member schools in their league.

But, in terms of a school having to become independent for five years before joining a different conference, the issue was brought up by Senator Moody that it could benefit schools like Florida State or Miami in her home state, along with a number of others that have taken issue with the ACC in previous years.

The amendment would provide a 180-day window for schools to opt-out of their current conference before the law would go into effect, if it actually ever does. But, this realignment provision provides schools the opportunity to avoid the 5-year independent clause and start the process of moving on without punishment.

If you think the ongoing issues between the NCAA and student-athletes suing for a fifth year of eligibility are wild, just wait until a number of schools try to jump ship and join a new conference before Christmas arrives.

Don't forget, Florida State and Clemson sued the ACC in 2023 over language in the conference's 'Grant of Rights' pertaining to how much it would cost for schools to leave before the ACC's television contract was set to expire.

While this might seem like a Senator doing her home-state school a solid, this 'independent' provision had already received pushback from plenty of leaders behind the scenes.

Whether those within Senate offices pushing for a bill to pass this week wanted to admit it, getting this to the floor for a vote was always a tall task, especially with time not on their side.

As of late afternoon Friday, there were 10 different holds and objections to the bill being expedited for a vote, with an additional eight holds pertaining to the PCSA on its own. Early Saturday morning, while there were still 'holds' (objections) to the bill, that number had been reduced considerably.

Without unanimous support, along with the 60 votes of support needed to pass the bill, an actual vote was still being worked on from those involved.

REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS

Senator John Kennedy (R-LA) took a shot at the legislation on Friday, aiming his comments towards providing the NCAA with enhanced protection that some do not want to provide on a broad basis.

"Make sure that this legislation doesn’t — either intentionally or unintentionally — absolve the NCAA, which lacks testicles and a spine, of any liability," Burgess Everrett reported.

Also, there was pushback from outside the nation's Capitol centered around the protection of women's sports under this legislation, with Riley Gaines writing that this bill in its current form has a 'fatal flaw', arguing that this would give transgender athletes legal grounds to challenge state eligibility rules.

Friday afternoon, White House counsel released a letter to congressional leaders emphasizing that the 'Protect College Sports Act' would not preempt current state laws that prohibit men for competing in women's sports.

"States may still legislate on the question of whether trans individuals should play on men's team or women's team."

And then, when you throw in the National Black Caucus releasing its own statement on not being able to support the bill in its current form, the likelihood of the PCSA actually garnering enough support started to feel as though it was slipping away in a more significant way.

This dragging into the college football season was always going to happen, no matter if the Senate took a vote this weekend or not.

The amendment process is going to take a lot more time than Friday provided, even if Senators decided to stick around for an additional day.

Then, if it passed through the Senate, there were going to be potential changes made in the House before a vote would take place on this part of the congressional ladder.

item.title: Dem Senate hopeful flip-flops on emerging issue impacting communities across US
item.description: Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown celebrated Amazon datacenter construction in Ohio in 2015 but now campaigns against them as an electric grid drain.
item.content:encoded:
Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, once praised data center expansion, records show, even as he now runs on a platform opposing their development in a bid to return to the Senate.

In 2015, Brown put out a press release celebrating the construction of a third data center in Central Ohio

"This new data center is great news for New Albany and central Ohio. Amazon’s growth in central Ohio signals that this region is not only a great place to do business, but a place where people want to live and raise a family," Brown said.

Now, just over 10 years later, Brown is painting Ohio’s 226 data centers as a drain on the state’s resources — a reversal that demonstrates how many Democrats have aligned themselves on the issue to press the case for affordability.

WATCH: GOP SENATOR UNLOADS ON 'CREATURE OF WASHINGTON' CHALLENGER IN CRITICAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

"Ohio’s electric grid — big corporations treat it like a game," Brown said in a recent campaign video.

"[They’re] gobbling up energy to feed their data centers no matter how much it raises our prices. It’s the latest way they’ve rigged the system."

Brown, who was originally elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006, lost re-election in 2024 to Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio. Now he is waging a comeback bid for Ohio’s other Senate seat against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted.

Husted, who has not yet won a full term in the Senate, was appointed by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine to fill the seat of now-former Sen. J.D. Vance, R-Ohio, when Trump tapped him to become vice president.

In the 2026 midterms, Democrats have hammered President Donald Trump and what they see as unfulfilled promises to bring down the cost of everyday items like food, fuel and housing.

While slightly removed from those specific items, an increasing number of Democrats, like Brown, have tied data centers to the issue, arguing that they do little to pay for their own costs in terms of water and electrical use. In their view, data centers are being subsidized by the communities where they’re being built.

FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC UNITY, REPUBLICAN CROSSOVERS SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE

Debates remain about whether their consumption has meaningfully changed utility rates in local communities and, if so, whether the companies should pay for the costs of their consumption.

Brown said he would support legislation along those lines.

"I’ll require the data centers to pay the full cost of their own electricity — not you," Brown said.

Ohio, in particular, has become an increasingly important state in the data center conversation as companies like Amazon and Google have sought out state incentives for their construction.

In 2013, the state legislature passed tax exemptions for the "sale, storage, use or other consumption of computer data center equipment." The law gives the Ohio Tax Credit Authority (TCA) the power to approve tax exemptions for companies that invest more than $100 million over three consecutive years. Not all centers are automatically qualified to participate in the benefit and can receive a partial exemption.

The move has attracted sizable investment but also cost the state $1.6 billion in forgone revenue in 2025, according to the Ohio 2026-2027 Tax Expenditure Report.

It’s unclear if Brown would support more than just a requirement that data centers pay for their electricity and whether he would consider other legislation to slow their development. In his 2015 press release, Brown noted that the centers had created new job opportunities with their openings.

TOP ENERGY GROUP WARNS WEALTHY FOREIGNERS ARE POTENTIALLY BANKROLLING ANTI-DATA CENTER CAMPAIGNS ACROSS US

"I look forward to working to ensure that our region’s burgeoning logistics hub continues to grow – creating good jobs for Ohioans and helping businesses prosper," Brown wrote.

His office did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital about the scope of his objections to data center developments in Ohio.

Having secured his party’s nomination for the seat, Brown will face Husted in the state’s Nov. 3 general election.

LINES WRAP AROUND BLOCK AS CUSTOMERS WAIT HOURS FOR VIRAL DOT CAKES THAT SELL OUT WITHIN MINUTES
