item.title: Morgan Fairchild says two men once abducted her off NYC street as bystanders laughed
item.description: Morgan Fairchild reveals on her new podcast how she joked her way to freedom in 1970 after being abducted off a New York City street while visiting her sister.
item.content:encoded:
Morgan Fairchild believes her sense of humor may have saved her life.

The actress, whose role on "Flamingo Road" cemented her bombshell image before she became a glamorous vixen on "Falcon Crest," has a new podcast, "2 B----es From Texas," co-hosted with her sister, Cathryn Hartt. The show features never-before-heard stories from their decades in showbiz and sit-down interviews with celebrity friends.

On a recent episode, Fairchild recalled being abducted on a New York City street before fame came calling. While it was no laughing matter, Fairchild said she managed to joke her way to freedom.

MORGAN FAIRCHILD REFUSED TO ‘SELL MY SOUL’ FOR HOLLYWOOD FAME

The then-20-year-old Dallas native was visiting her sister in 1970 when the terrifying ordeal unfolded.

"I'm walking up at two o'clock in the afternoon, broad daylight, no reason to be scared," Fairchild recalled to Fox News Digital.

"And this one big guy comes up talking to me. Now, I'm from Texas, but I know you're not supposed to talk to people on the street in New York. You don't talk to gentlemen. So I'm just ignoring him. And then this other big guy comes up on the other side of me. And these guys are both over six feet tall. They just grabbed me up by the elbows and threw me in this cab that was loitering there that I hadn't noticed."

WATCH: LORENZO LAMAS SHARES HOW HE MANAGES THE PRESSURES OF FAME

Fairchild said several people were waiting at a nearby bus stop, while others were walking by. Realizing she was in danger, she screamed for help. Fairchild said they must have thought she was "a hooker or something."

"Nobody lifted a finger," she said. "In fact, some of them laughed. And that made me realize how easy it would be to totally disappear and nobody would ever know what happened to you."

"The cab has very thick plexiglass between the passengers and the driver," Fairchild recalled. "I don't think the driver spoke much English. But these guys started telling me all the things they were going to do to me. That's how I found out that one was a pimp and the other was a pusher. The one who was a pusher was telling me all the things he was going to shoot me up with. And the pimp was telling me all the things that he was going to do to my body."

"I was a shy kid, but I was damned if I was going to let them see how scared I was," Fairchild added.

Fairchild said that every time her abductors described what they were going to do to her, she responded with "a wisecrack."

"I had them laughing," Fairchild said. "At one point, unbelievably to me, one of them looked at the other and said, 'She's funny. Let's let her go.' And they did. They gave the cab driver some money and said, 'Take her wherever she wants to go.' Well, I went back to my sister's apartment."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I didn't come out for three days," she admitted. "Intro to New York 101. It was very, very scary."

Fairchild still wonders how she managed to think so quickly while fearing for her life.

"I have no clue," she said. "It was all intuitive because I was not going to let them see how scared I was. That's what I did. I had to talk my way out of it by being funny, just being a wise a--. It's like an improvisation class. Somebody says something, and you come up with something else and make the scene work. It's like that, only much more dangerous. I've talked my way out of things a couple of times in my life just by being a wise a--."

"My sister had been living in New York for a little bit," she said. "I was the naïve one from Texas. Although naïve doesn't really cover it because I wasn't doing anything stupid. I was just walking in broad daylight. It wasn't in a dark alley, coming out of a club drunk or any of those other things that could make you vulnerable."

Fairchild said she shared the story on her podcast to encourage women to be aware of their surroundings.

"I think what women really need to keep in mind is how easy it is for you to just disappear," said Fairchild. "People were laughing at me as they were throwing me into this car. That, to me, was one of the scariest things: the lack of feeling for your fellow man. And you don’t think something like this could really ever happen to you."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The experience has stayed with Fairchild. To this day, she keeps watch on her surroundings.

"I always scan buildings," she said. "I keep an eye out all the time to see if I'm being followed. I do it surreptitiously, so people don't really realize, but I'm watching. I'm checking things in a rearview mirror. If I'm in a building, I check to see where the exits are. You have to be aware of your surroundings."

"I say this to women because they're always on their cell phones and that makes them so vulnerable," Fairchild continued.

"They're not paying attention to what's going on around them. They're not paying attention to who's following them, whether somebody could be hiding around a corner. I'm now very aware all the time. I never walk and text. And that's what I tell women. Never walk and text. A lot of young women tend to make that mistake. When you walk and text, you become so unaware of anything around you that's happening. You're assuming that you're safe. Never assume that you're safe."

Beyond revisiting stories from her past, Fairchild said she hopes the podcast encourages listeners to show more kindness.

"It's been really fun getting to connect with friends again," Fairchild said. "And it's fun that our listeners are reacting to these stories. And you know, on my social media, I sign off with the hashtag #bekind. And I think that's one thing that's missing in our society these days: kindness and trying to understand other people's points of view."

item.title: Colorado's socialist surge shakes up the Democratic establishment
item.description: A veteran Colorado political insider warned the Democratic Socialists' rise in Denver mirrors the MAGA movement and could become a cancer for Democrats.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros shocked Colorado’s Democratic establishment when she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the state's June primary. The double-digit win exposed a growing rift over the party's values that has left some Democrats stunned and questioning the future of the party.

"If you had told me this woman would have won by 13 points, I would have bet my house against that," Doug Friednash, a veteran political strategist in Colorado, told Fox News Digital. "I never would have thought we would have seen a victory of that magnitude here in Denver."

Friednash has tracked Colorado's political shift from red to deep blue over the past three decades, previously serving in the state legislature representing House District 10 in Denver. He later served as Denver city attorney and chief of staff to former Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, and he currently works as a partner at Brownstein, a prominent legal and lobbying firm in the region.

Kiros' victory was one of dozens of wins for far-left candidates in Democratic primary elections this cycle as socialists continue to ascend across the country. The far-left's rise in the party has alarmed seasoned Democrats like Friednash.

JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS

"It was one thing watching this happen in New York ... But when it happens in a state like Colorado, which is really the gateway to the West, it tells me that this issue is going to spread and may be a cancer to the Democratic Party if they don't figure out what our values are," Friednash said.

He noted that Kiros' victory did not happen in a vacuum, pointing out that DSA-backed candidates have successfully captured seats in the state legislature and city councils over the past few years.

While Friednash originally predicted Rep. Diana DeGette would win, he acknowledged Kiros' campaign had a strong ground game and was able to tap into anti-establishment sentiments among progressives in the region. Kiros' team reportedly knocked on more than 100,000 voters' doors and ran a phone bank reaching 500,000 people leading up to election night.

SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM

She also campaigned on fighting for universal healthcare, affordable housing, utilities and more.

Friednash said Kiros' message resonated with younger voters who are frustrated by the high cost of living and feel let down by the Democratic establishment.

"I think the number one issue is affordability, by far," he said. "A lot of younger people that have moved to Denver have come here wanting to buy a house. They can't buy a home, it seems unaffordable and unattainable. And I think she's tapped into a lot of voter anger and hostility over things not being better."

He believes Denver has become a microcosm of the national debate taking place within the Democratic Party over its future direction. Comparing the DSA wave to the rise of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, Friednash warned that if party leadership refuses to call out the group's extreme policies, it will ultimately hurt Democrats in swing districts across the nation.

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN'

"As I look out at what's happening within the Democratic Party, you know, it's kind of like a ship without a captain," Friednash said. "A lot of the more mainstream Democrats, rather than trying to say, 'Here are the issues we should be fighting about,' are embracing the socialists, because I think they're afraid of them... much like I think we've seen with the MAGA movement."

"While some Democrats may be falling in love with socialism, you know who isn't? The rest of America," he continued. "That dog's not gonna hunt in these more competitive primaries."

Prominent centrist Democratic groups such as Third Way share that anxiety. The organization recently told The New York Times it plans to launch a $15 million campaign to combat the Democratic Socialists of America movement, which it believes poses a "mortal danger" to Democrats and will hurt the party in potential presidential swing states.

Concerns over the party's ideological turn aren't limited to establishment Democrats.

Jon Caldara, president of the Denver-based free-market think tank Independence Institute, also questions the future of his home state as democratic socialists continue to rise in prominence.

"Without a doubt, the Democratic Party in Colorado has changed," Caldara told Fox News Digital, arguing the state has abandoned its historically pro-business stance.

Caldara, a libertarian and longtime radio host and columnist, is outspoken about the challenges facing Denver and the broader state, such as affordability, homelessness and an exodus of businesses. He believes these issues will worsen, warning that establishment Democrats have lost control of their own party.

"When the state started turning left, this machine was so powerful, it really couldn't stop itself," Caldara said. "And now it's really beginning to eat their own. It's kind of a French Revolution thing that you see that the Democratic Party here in Colorado is now well out over their skis. And there is a growing fight between Democrats and socialists."

"The real telltale is that Democrats are afraid to speak the truth because they don't want to get canceled," he added. "It is vicious to go against the socialists."

SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'

Caldara believes younger voters are increasingly being drawn to democratic socialist candidates in Denver and across the country because they lack historical context for how these types of policies have fared across the world.

"Sadly, the young suffer from a terrible disease: It's called youth. And because they're young, they haven't seen failed socialism around the globe," Caldara said. "They haven't seen what happened in the Soviet Union. They haven't learned the lesson of Sweden, which looked like such a wonderful socialist paradise until it didn't work, and now they're turning into a capitalist system. They haven't seen this."

"So the idea that we can just redistribute rich guys' money sounds great," he continued. "We'll just do rent control. We'll do government funding. We all know how that's going to end up. It's going to end up poorly. And young people are going to be hurt."

"I'm sad that they want to run this experiment again," he added. "And it's even sadder that it's happening in this beautiful free state, this western state, this pro-free-enterprise state of Colorado."

Longtime Colorado residents like Gene Maine understand full well why socialist policies are appealing. But having fled the Soviet Union as a teenager in 1981, Maine sees unsettling parallels between the society he grew up in and the direction Denver is headed.

As a child, Maine said he was often told that America, Western Europe and capitalism were evil. But as he got older, he realized the utopian society he was supposedly living in wasn't all that it was cracked up to be.

REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP'

"As I grew older, I started recognizing that, ‘Oh my God, I'm being lied to. We're all being lied to," Maine recalled. "This is not the freest society in the world. It's a jail."

After defecting from the USSR with his mother as a teenager, Maine lived in Los Angeles before settling in Erie, Colorado in the 1990s, where he’s lived since, raising his family and working as an engineer.

Over the past three decades, Maine has watched Denver change from a small "cow town" into a large municipality, and witnessed a corresponding political shift as the population boomed.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

"All of a sudden, it wasn't, 'Can we have the smallest government possible and leave us alone?' It became, 'Well, we need to give you free stuff.' And that's when I started to worry a little bit," Maine said.

Maine isn't surprised that veteran Democrats are facing primary threats from the far left, noting that Kiros’ campaign benefited from a well-organized ground game and sweeping promises on healthcare and affordability that drew in younger voters.

"She is winning the primary because we have an organized group convincing people that they can have free stuff. You can have free medical care. You can have free supermarkets. You can have free transportation. And it's very appealing," Maine explained. "I like free stuff, but what they forget to tell you is that nothing is really free. As they say, there's no free lunch."

SOCIALIST HOUSE CANDIDATE SAYS HE AGREES WITH REPUBLICANS ON 'ONE ISSUE'

He believes historical lessons are being lost as generations grow further removed from the realities of the Soviet Union.

"So there is a gap that's being exploited," he continued. "And it's been exploited from internal and from external, because there's a lot of evil forces in the world that do not want America to succeed."

While critics view the rise of the DSA as a dangerous departure from American values, Kiros and other DSA candidates argue their policies are a pragmatic response to liberal voters fed up with how the Democratic Party has responded to their struggles.

Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS’s "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover that there is room in the party for various viewpoints.

"Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right?"

"Until a self-proclaimed communist actually wins an election, then it’s just noise from the Republican Party. There’s no one who’s actually winning with that," she continued.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Kiros denied being a communist herself, arguing that younger voters are embracing the DSA message because, at its core, it represents "economic populism."

Her campaign centered on Medicare for all, universal childcare, investments in public housing, higher federal taxes on the wealthy, publicly owned utilities and more. Like many other socialist campaigns across the country, she is also firmly anti-Israel. 

Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats, and the Working Families Party.

Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77 percent of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado.

Kiros’s campaign and the DSA did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: Socialist wave 'ripping America apart' will hit a wall with Michigan voters: Rising star House candidate
item.description: Mike Bouchard Jr. slams Abdul El-Sayed's campaign with Hasan Piker and vows Michigan voters will reject socialism in the 10th Congressional District.
item.content:encoded:
WARREN, MI - Mike Bouchard Jr., the Republican nominee for Michigan's 10th Congressional District, says Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow Senate primary victory is no sign Michigan as a whole is embracing socialism and that the progressive Democrat's message is dividing the country.

"El-Sayed was campaigning with Hasan Piker the day before the election, Hasan Piker said that America deserved 9/11, we did not deserve 9/11, tell that to the thousands of people who died in 9/11 and the thousands of American military who died abroad defending this country," Bouchard, a Bronze Star recipient who served as an infantry officer in the 101st Airborne Division and an intelligence officer in the 82nd Airborne Division, told Fox News Digital.

"The fact that that is coming to our streets, that someone says that America deserves something like that, that is ripping America apart block by block. We need to come together, build this country up, and find real solutions together. I'm done with this partisan politics and trying to bring socialism into a country that is not what we were founded on."

El-Sayed was crowned the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Michigan on Tuesday night, winning a razor-thin contest by less than a percentage point against the establishment-backed Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens.

EL-SAYED PALS AROUND WITH FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER THE DAY BEFORE CRUCIAL MICHIGAN SENATE ELECTION

Bouchard told Fox News Digital that El-Sayed’s victory shows a "split" in the Democratic Party but said that while the socialist wing is the "loudest voice" in the room, he doesn’t believe most Michigan voters are swayed by far-left politicians.

"Absolutely not," Bouchard said. "The people in Michigan are hard workers. They work hard, they love their families, and you know what? They're moderates. They go back and forth. They look at Democrats, they'll look at Republicans. They don't want partisan politics. They want someone who's going to deliver results for them. And that's why I got in this race is to deliver real, meaningful results."

Bouchard, the son of longtime Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard, reacted to the much talked-about socialist wave in the Democratic Party as far-left candidates win across the country, and now in the Midwest with candidates like El-Sayed and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong.

EL-SAYED CAMPAIGN BACKED BY OVER $100,000 FROM DOZENS OF MEMBERS OF GROUP WITH ALLEGED TERROR TIES

"When the Berlin wall came down, which way did the people run?" Bouchard said. "Did they run towards a communist Soviet union, or did they run towards freedom in America? Socialism doesn't work. It's been proven time and time again. I've fought all across the world and I've seen what socialism does to a country. We cannot allow that to come here."

"Yes, I'm running for change, but socialism is not the answer, and so Abdul El-Sayed stands for defunding the police. And it's been really interesting to see how my opponent, who's soft on crime, works with El-Sayed when he's trying to tear this country down. I want to build this country up."

Bouchard will face Democrat Christina Hines, a former county prosecutor, in November after he won Tuesday night’s GOP primary to replace Rep. John James, who is running for governor, in Congress. Bouchard told Fox News Digital that the contrast between him and Hines on crime will be a main focus of his.

Hines has faced criticism from her Republican opponents on the crime issue and Bouchard said Hines "stands for soft on crime policies and a woke agenda that I just don't align with."

" You look across a lot of the prosecutors across the country, some enforce the rules on the books, some don't, some blame victims, and some are really kind to the offenders, I stand for protecting victims and making sure that the offenders go to prison," Bouchard said. "And so I've seen people praise my opponent for being kind and compassionate to offenders. I stand for the victims. People in this district want to be safe and if you're not safe, you can't do anything else. You can't leave your house. So from the southern border to crime across the district, I'm gonna stand up for the people of this district."

Hines pushed back on Bouchard’s criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, contrasting her career as a prosecutor with Bouchard’s military background.

"Mike Bouchard Jr has never put a predator behind bars, and he’s never lived in Macomb a day in his life. I spent my entire career working with law enforcement to put serial rapists, child predators, murderers, and traffickers in prison. I’m running for Congress to protect the families in my community, and to fight against the corruption that’s rampant in DC."

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.
